newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African manufacturing confidence falls - BER.
newsitem.headline: South African manufacturing confidence falls - BER.

text.p: South African manufacturers' unrealistically high expectations of business conditions in the second half of the year have failed to materialise, the University of Stellenbosch's Bureau for Economic Research said on Thursday.
It blamed this on the fact that the general situation in the retail and wholesale sectors could not sustain the sharp improvement in manufacturing volumes seen in the first quarter.
"It is possible that the recent appreciation of the rand was (also) detrimental to exports and had a sobering effect on manufacturers' export expectations," BER said in a statement.
Instead of accelerating in the second quarter, the growth in domestic and export sales and order volumes slowed down.
"As a result, finished goods stocks accumulated and production growth was curtailed," it said.
The unrealised expectations had a major impact on business confidence and the business confidence index fell to 38 from 53 out of 100, or close to the level in the third quarter of 1996.

BER said stocks of finished goods were now unsatisfactorily high, indicating downward pressure on production and factory employment in the months ahead. In addition, the delivery periods of orders received shortened.
But manufacturers said they did not expect a sharp fall in sales and production volumes.
"Although the overall results point to a significant slowdown in the second quarter, it is still encouraging that the underlying improving trend remains in place," BER said.

"Expectations regarding the domestic market have been adjusted to more realistic levels and indicate sustained year-on-year growth. But it is unlikely for business conditions to improve significantly in the forecast quarter.

"On balance, manufacturers remain optimistic regarding the growth of export volumes in the 12 months ahead. Import expectations and plans to invest in machinery and equipment also reveal underlying optimism."
On South Africa's short term economic prospects, BER said real domestic expenditure was clearly in a downswing.

Private consumption expenditure and business investor investment could be sluggish for the greater part of 1997, while growth in fixed investment expenditure could be sustained, albeit at lower levels than in 1996.
"The short-term export outlook remains favourable, despite manufacturers' revised expectations and the strength of the rand during the first half of 1997," BER said.

Much would, however, depend on demand conditions in the economies of major trading partners. These looked favourable and were likely to assist export-led domestic economic recovery towards the end of the year and in 1998.
